title: Paul Tremaine's band and early swing impressions
summary: Kmen recalls the Paul Tremaine band as a relaxed forerunner of swing, compared with Casa Loma.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: That's funny, I don't remember anything about him at all.

Well, we've talked about this at other times, Nick, and it really doesn't belong here, but somebody, someday, ought to dig into the big bands in America too. That whole era of bands before it's lost completely. You remember I often mention to you my favorite band up there, the Lonely Acres Band, and young Chinese Paul Tremaine and his Lonely Acres Band. I've never seen reference one to that any place. And I remember that band so well coming on the radio at noontime when I was a kid still in school, and playing tunes like Hand Me Down My Walking Cane and everything, big band swing style. And he did spirituals too, didn't he, Tremaine? Well, yeah, what was it called? Well, they'd do things like semi-spirrors, you know, gold and slippers, and maybe swing low sweet cherry, things like that.

Swinging them all. Did you ever know a fellow named Teddy Brewer, he later called himself Teddy Martin, he played Albert System clarinet on Bourbon Street, a non-human about 1950, I forget what happened to him. Fudd was playing piano with him some it seems to me, and a guy who played valve trombone, he told me something about Paul Tremaine.
Well, I'd like to meet him then, because that's the only other guy I've ever heard of that heard of Paul Tremaine, and yet I can tell you that band was...
Yeah, I've heard of him. Paul Barber and then he were talking about what that, I just remember. About Paul Tremaine's band? About Tremaine's band. Then I'd like to ask Barber about it.

Yeah, well I remember that was a very popular band. I know they were in Young's Chinese American restaurant in New York for years, and they must have come previously from someplace called Only Acres, maybe a dance hall or something, you know, they did that off, like the Casa Loma Band came out of a Casa Loma restaurant. And I understood later on that the guys were working there for about seventeen dollars a week and found a room and board, which was not uncommon for bands in those days, you used to work for very very little. Twelve, fifteen dollars a week and a room and board. And I don't know what ever became of that band. But I remember this, that at a time when the outstanding swing band, this is in the pre-swing era, if you could even call it that, a swing band, but jazz band or a big jazz band, as far as the public was concerned, was the Casa Loma Band. When you'd hear Tremaine, you'd recognize already that this was in advance in the loose, relaxed swing it had, much more like the later swing bands.
I didn't have that impression of it. I thought it was much more rikki-tikki and stiff in its rhythm, but it wasn't.

Well, again, not having records so that you can go back. Yeah. You know, I've heard recently some Goodman records that I remember distinctly, and this is later, in 1937, 38, I thought were great swinging things. And I hear them now and they sound pretty heavy and sodden with rhythm. So you never know what your impressions are like, but I remember this impression about the Tremaine band distinctly, that for its time, it seemed to me like an advance group that the loose swing had.
I have to find some records about them. I guess I will. I think I may have one at one time or another, but I may have had one.

I was hearing at the same time Don Redmond and bands like that, Jimmy Lunsford. Not very often though, you see, because the radio didn't play at Jimmy Lunsford or Don Redmond as often as you could get a band like Paul Tremaine, except because of the hotel situation.
